summary:
Team NOVALITH developed Mars Explorer, an interactive web prototype for planning a simulated science traverse across the western delta of Jezero Crater. It addresses the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge by combining NASA orbital imagery, HiRISE elevation data, USGS regional geology, and Perseverance observations in one layered map.

Users can explore science sites, choose a start and destination, and compare routes by distance and slope. When a route crosses a simulated dust storm, the app can calculate a detour and show how the change affects travel time and estimated oxygen and battery reserves. A shared Mission Control view lets teammates follow the simulated traverse and discuss route decisions.

The shortest route can cross steep terrain or a hazard, while a detour can use more time and resources. Mars Explorer makes those trade-offs visible and gives students and teams a practical way to explore how real planetary data can inform a simulated mission.
details:
How it works

Team NOVALITH built Mars Explorer for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. It is a web prototype for planning and simulating science traverses in a roughly 2 × 2 km area of Jezero Crater’s western delta. The map combines NASA/JPL orbital imagery, HiRISE stereo elevation data, USGS regional geology, and observations from the Perseverance rover.

Users can switch map layers, inspect a point’s elevation and slope, and explore science sites such as Skinner Ridge. In Route Planner, they select a start and destination, add optional waypoints, and compare the shortest route with an alternative that accounts for slope. The app displays distance, maximum sampled grade, an elevation profile, and nearby science sites.

What makes it creative

The map turns a route into a decision users can test. They can add a simulated dust storm, see whether it intersects the planned route, and calculate a detour. The app shows how route choices affect estimated travel time, oxygen, and battery reserves. During a simulated traverse, teammates can use a mission code to follow progress in Mission Control. They can also report a route obstacle and review or replay the traverse afterward.

In one test of the hosted app, the weather detour avoided the simulated storm and added about 71 meters, while reducing the maximum sampled grade from 22.3° to 16.3°. That example shows why we made both distance and terrain effort visible.

Tools, design choices, and intended impact

We built the interface with JavaScript, React, HTML, and CSS, using OpenLayers for mapping and Three.js for 3D views. Python and FastAPI handle terrain sampling and route calculations. Vercel hosts the app, and Neon PostgreSQL stores shared missions and incident reports. The prototype runs in a standard web browser.

We considered map alignment, terrain resolution, access to science targets, uncertainty in resource estimates, and availability of live NASA feeds. The core route planner uses bundled terrain data. The approximately 20 m analysis grid cannot resolve small obstacles or soil strength, and the simulated hazards and suit estimates cannot establish astronaut safety. Our goal is to help students and teams understand how planetary data informs route decisions and explain why a plan changes when conditions change.
